summary: Auroraa is an offline-first astronaut health and spacewalk-readiness system that runs onboard the spacecraft, with a working dashboard prototype showing how a crew member would use it. As crews travel farther from Earth, the radio delay stretches from seconds at the Moon to about 20 minutes at Mars, so flight surgeons can no longer monitor astronauts in real time — and the earliest warning signs of trouble (fatigue, dehydration, a lapse in attention, shaky hands) are the easiest to miss. Auroraa turns those scattered signals into one clear go / no-go decision: a guided pre-spacewalk checklist and physical, neurological and environmental clearance; quick daily gamified check-ins for reaction time, working memory, fine-motor stability and mood; and onboard sensor data on heart rhythm, temperature, circadian rhythm, hydration and exercise load. Everything is processed at the edge, so it keeps working through communication blackouts and syncs only summaries to mission control. That gives crews the autonomy to decide safely alone, and Earth a trustworthy low-bandwidth picture of crew health — a design that also transfers to diving, aviation, remote industry and rural clinics.
details:
Auroraa is an offline-first astronaut health and spacewalk (EVA) readiness system. Its main use is the moment before a spacewalk: a crew member works through a guided readiness protocol at a console and receives a single, explained go / no-go decision, produced onboard from their own recent health data instead of waiting for a reply from Earth. It addresses the loss of real-time medical supervision as crews travel farther out. Communication delay grows from seconds in low Earth orbit to roughly 20 minutes at Mars, and the earliest warning signs of trouble — fatigue, dehydration, a lapse in attention, a small loss of hand stability — are exactly what is easy to miss over a delayed, low-bandwidth link.

The delivered project is a working, interactive web prototype of the crew dashboard. It includes a mission shell with navigation, status chips and crew profile; a telemetry grid with live panels for ECG, thermal and circadian trends, hydration, cognition and exercise load; a body-status stage that marks the flagged system with biomarker hotspots; and a mission-critical row consolidating alerts, readiness status and recommended actions. Alerts escalate from nominal to caution to critical with the reason in plain language rather than raw numbers. The layout is responsive down to a 390 px phone width and exposes keyboard focus states, and all artwork is served locally so the interface renders with no network connection. The readiness protocol itself is also specified and demonstrated: automated equipment checklist, physical check, neurological screening (reaction time, working memory, fine-motor stability), environmental clearance and a daily well-being self-report.

The design is a three-layer edge system. Wearable and suit sensors plus short crew tests produce timestamped measurements — heart rhythm, temperature, circadian phase, hydration, exercise load, reaction time, memory accuracy, tap stability and mood. Onboard compute compares each against the crew member's own rolling baseline rather than a population average, because individual baselines are far more informative for a small crew. A readiness score is computed from weighted cardiovascular, thermal, hydration, cognitive, motor and psychological domains, and any domain crossing its threshold produces a plain-language reason and an action. Only a compact summary, never the raw stream, is queued for mission control when a link exists. In practice, a crew member who slept poorly, is mildly dehydrated and shows slower reaction time and less stable tapping than their own baseline receives a caution naming those reasons plus an action such as rehydration, rest or repeating the motor test; if every domain is inside baseline, the result is a clear go.

The benefit is autonomy under delay: the crew can decide safely during a communication blackout, when a 20-minute round trip is unacceptable, while flight surgeons still receive a decision-ready picture. Personalised trend baselines catch drift a single reading would miss, and one explained decision replaces a wall of telemetry for a tired crew member. The same architecture transfers to diving, aviation, remote industrial sites and rural clinics.

The front end is React and TypeScript with a custom design system (dark obsidian base, aurora-green accent, Space Grotesk and Inter), charts and the body stage drawn as scalable vectors, locally bundled assets and no external CDN dependency at runtime. Data is simulated in the prototype but shaped to match real sensor fields. Domain framing follows NASA Human Research Program hazard and risk categories and Canadian Space Agency life-science material. The prototype runs in a browser; the intended target is radiation-tolerant onboard compute with wearable and suit sensor feeds, and no flight hardware was built.

Limitations are stated plainly. Thresholds and weights are engineering heuristics informed by published risk domains, not clinically validated cutoffs, so Auroraa is decision support rather than a medical device and does not replace a flight surgeon. The prototype runs on simulated telemetry with no real astronaut or suit data and no sensor integration; the cognitive and motor tasks are faithful in spirit but not formally calibrated; and there is no radiation qualification, flight certification or security hardening, with offline sync and multi-crew support designed but not implemented. Future work covers sensor integration and a hardware bench prototype, per-crew baseline learning with drift detection, mission-control and clinician views, encrypted store-and-forward sync, and an Earth pilot in a high-risk operations or rural care setting
